title: Stop Guessing. Measure Your Maths Instruction.
author: Brendan Lee
source: Knowledge for Teachers on Substack, December 8, 2025
summary: Lee makes a leadership-focused argument for diagnostic clarity before strategic decision-making, grounded in the teacher-effectiveness literature (Muijs, Timperley, Antoniou). The core claim: most school improvement decisions are made before the problem is properly described. Schools select professional learning, adopt programs, and change routines without a shared, evidence-informed picture of what is actually happening in classrooms. When the need is externally defined rather than locally diagnosed, teachers experience the goals as belonging to someone else, engagement becomes optional, and change stays shallow. The instrument Lee points to is his Effective Maths Instruction Scorecard. In under fifteen minutes, a leadership team rates nine elements of instruction: retrieval practice, modelling, guided practice, independent practice, opportunities to respond, lesson structure, and alignment to the stage of learning. Each element is described across four levels from emerging to highly effective. The total score is not the point. What the score makes visible is. The descriptors create a shared reference so that debates about whether modelling is 'good enough' give way to pointing at specific indicators of what modelling looks like at a given level. The piece is pitched at primary leaders planning for next year, and Lee's practical recommendation is restraint. End-of-year is not the moment to launch new initiatives, it is the moment to take stock. Patterns cluster predictably: modelling may be strong while guided practice varies, retrieval may be present but inconsistent, independent practice may be released too early in some classrooms and too late in others. Those patterns are more useful than a long list of unrelated improvement goals. The scorecard's suggested next steps do not ask for new programs, only tightened routines, clarified expectations, and closer alignment between teaching and stage of learning. The discipline, as he puts it, is measure before you modify.
points: The central argument of this piece is grounded in the author's engagement with how real people think and act, not in idealized or abstract reasoning.
The takeaway is actionable,it can be implemented at the classroom or school level without waiting for policy change or external resources.
The piece challenges a common default assumption in education practice and offers a concrete alternative framed by evidence or lived experience.
The stakes are clear: what happens if leaders or teachers adopt this approach, and what is the cost of continuing the current default.
quotes: Most conversations about improving maths instruction begin with assumptions. We assume certain routines are in place, that modelling is clear or that students are getting enough practice. In reality, improvement starts when we stop guessing and describe what is actually happening in classrooms.

One of the most persistent problems in school improvement is that decisions are often made before the problem is properly described. Professional learning is selected, programs are adopted and new practices are introduced without a clear understanding of what is actually happening in classrooms.

When the need is externally defined, goals belong to others. Teachers are asked to engage with ideas without first understanding why they matter or how they connect to their own practice. Engagement becomes optional, resistance becomes understandable and change remains shallow.

Research consistently shows that professional learning has the greatest impact when it is tightly focused on specific challenges, grounded in classroom evidence and linked directly to student outcomes rather than abstract principles (Antoniou et al., 2015; Timperley et al., 2008).

Improvement does not start with choosing what to do next. It starts with accurately describing what is happening now. Without that clarity, even well intentioned decisions are unlikely to lead to meaningful change.

What matters is not the total score itself. What matters is what the score makes visible. The descriptors provide a common reference point. Instead of debating whether modelling is “good enough”, leaders can point to specific indicators that describe what modelling actually looks like at different levels of quality.

The end of the year is rarely the right moment to introduce new initiatives. It is, however, the ideal time to take stock. Completing the scorecard now allows leadership teams to step back from day to day pressures and look for patterns.

If you are planning for next year, start with restraint. Measure before you modify. Describe before you decide. Choose one priority that genuinely matters. Improvement does not begin with new initiatives. It begins with clarity.” Archived from Knowledge for Teachers on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
